heard: Forty-three instruments laid out three ways. These are design layouts, not built labs.  First, a conventional materials lab, grouped by workflow.  Rooms for powder, the metal printers, the machine shop, the furnace and the SEM, and open benches for the rest.  Benches are 30 inches deep and aisles 5 feet wide, with service space behind every floor machine.  Measured to its walls, it comes to 4,280 square feet.  Next, the same floor plan, automated.  Mobile robots drive the routes people walked, with fixed arms, docking targets and sample racks at the stations.  The floor area stays the same, and a robot docked in a 5-foot aisle leaves too little room for another to pass.  The vertical lab, two cardiac shuttles come in, and every benchtop instrument moves onto a tray.  The floor machines rearrange along one robot aisle, and the floor area falls to 3,029 square feet.  Side by side, the vertical lab needs 29% less floor, 14.2 instruments per 1,000 square feet, against 10.0.  Most of what is left is floor machines, their clearances and the robot aisle.  And the shuttles stand 9.15 meters tall, so it needs a high bay.  For scale, Emerald Cloud Lab in South, San Francisco held more than 100 items of equipment in about 15,000 square feet.
